title: Huffman Coding — Greedy with a Min-Heap
summary: Building an optimal prefix code by greedily merging the two rarest symbols with a min-heap — the group's most compelling exchange argument, and where greedy meets heaps directly.

slides.markdown:
Huffman coding builds an optimal **prefix code** — a way to assign variable-length bit strings to symbols so that frequent symbols get short codes and rare symbols get longer ones, minimizing total encoded length. The algorithm: repeatedly merge the two least-frequent remaining symbols into a combined node, until one tree remains.

It's the group's closing topic for a reason: it combines a real greedy insight (why merging the *two rarest* is always safe) with a data structure this curriculum has already covered (`heaps`), and its exchange argument is genuinely more interesting than most — it argues about tree *depth*, not just a numeric value, which is a step up from every earlier proof in this group.

slides.sectionTitle: Why prefix-free codes need no delimiter
slides.markdown:
A **prefix-free** (or prefix) code guarantees no code word is a prefix of another. That single property is what lets a decoder read a bitstream left to right and know exactly when one symbol's code ends and the next begins, with no separator character needed.

Without the prefix-free guarantee, a code like `{a: 0, b: 01}` is ambiguous — the bitstream `01` could be `a` followed by `1` (invalid, or the start of something else) or just `b`. Huffman's tree structure enforces prefix-freeness automatically: every symbol sits at a **leaf**, and a leaf's path from the root can never be a prefix of another leaf's path, since prefixes correspond to internal nodes, not other leaves.

Start with one leaf node per symbol, weighted by its frequency, all sitting in a min-heap keyed by weight. Repeatedly pop the two smallest, create a new internal node whose weight is their sum and whose two children are the popped nodes, and push it back in. The last node remaining is the tree's root.

![Four leaf frequencies 5, 9, 12, 13 merging step by step into 14, then 26, then the final root 39](assets/huffman-tree-build.svg)

Each merge step reduces the number of "active" nodes in the heap by one, so after exactly `n - 1` merges (for `n` symbols), a single tree remains.

assets.alt: Four leaf frequencies 5, 9, 12, 13 merging step by step into 14, then 26, then the final root 39

slides.markdown:
The claim to prove: the two rarest symbols can always be placed at the **deepest level** of *some* optimal tree, as siblings. The exchange argument: take any optimal tree where this isn't already true. Find whatever symbols currently sit at the deepest level, and swap them with the two rarest symbols, wherever those currently sit.

Because the two rarest symbols have the smallest frequencies, moving them to the deepest (longest-code) positions and moving whatever was there to a shallower position can only **decrease or maintain** the total weighted code length — a large frequency multiplied by a shorter depth, plus a small frequency multiplied by a longer depth, is always at least as good as the reverse pairing. This is a genuinely different flavor of exchange argument from earlier in this group: it's arguing about **structural position in a tree**, not about a numeric value directly.

| | Fixed-length code | Huffman (variable-length) |
|---|---|---|
| Code length per symbol | Same for every symbol (e.g. always 3 bits for 8 symbols) | Shorter for frequent symbols, longer for rare ones |
| Total encoded length | frequency-agnostic — same regardless of symbol distribution | Minimized for the actual observed frequency distribution |
| Where savings come from | None — no distribution-awareness | Frequent symbols repeatedly "pay" fewer bits each occurrence |

The savings scale with how skewed the frequency distribution is: a near-uniform distribution gives Huffman little advantage over fixed-length coding (it may even converge to nearly the same code lengths), while a highly skewed distribution (a few very common symbols, many rare ones) can produce dramatic savings — this is exactly why Huffman coding is a real building block inside general-purpose compression formats.

O(n log n): `n - 1` merge rounds, each doing two heap pops and one heap push, all O(log n) on a heap of size up to `n`. This is driven entirely by the heap operations — the merging logic itself (summing two weights, linking two nodes) is O(1) per round.

Worth stating explicitly if asked to compare to alternatives: without a heap, repeatedly finding "the two smallest remaining" via linear scan would be O(n²) total — the heap is doing real work here, not just a convenient implementation detail, and it's the direct reason this problem sits at the intersection of the `greedy` and `heaps` groups.

slides.sectionTitle: Ties change the tree, not the optimality
slides.markdown:
When two or more symbols (or merged nodes) tie in frequency, the choice of which pair to merge first can produce a **different tree** — different code words assigned to different symbols — while the **total weighted code length stays optimal** either way. Assuming a tie means "something went wrong" or that one specific tie-breaking rule is required for correctness is a misunderstanding of what the algorithm actually guarantees.

The guarantee is on the objective (total length), not on which specific tree you get — multiple optimal trees can coexist. If a problem's grader expects one specific tree, that's an artifact of a specific tie-breaking convention (often "prefer the earlier-inserted node" or similar), not a mathematical requirement of Huffman coding itself, and worth clarifying if the exact tree shape (not just its cost) is being checked.

slides.sectionTitle: Reading codes off the finished tree
slides.markdown:
Once the tree is built, each symbol's code word is the sequence of left/right choices (conventionally `0` for left, `1` for right) along the path from the root to that symbol's leaf. This can be read off in a single traversal after construction, rather than needing to be tracked incrementally during every merge (though the earlier code slide did track it incrementally, which also works and avoids a second pass).

A symbol that ends up at depth 2 gets a 2-bit code; one at depth 5 gets a 5-bit code — and by construction (from the exchange argument), the rarest symbols are the ones pushed to the deepest, longest-code positions, while the most frequent symbols end up shallow with short codes.

Decoding walks the tree from the root, following each incoming bit (left on `0`, right on `1`) until a leaf is reached — that leaf's symbol is emitted, and the walk restarts from the root for the next bit. The prefix-free property guarantees this never needs lookahead: there's no ambiguity about when one symbol's code ends, because no complete code word is ever a prefix of another.

This is O(length of the bitstream) — each bit is processed exactly once, moving one step down the tree, with no backtracking needed. The simplicity of the decoder is a direct consequence of the prefix-free structure this topic opened with, not a separate algorithm to design from scratch.

slides.sectionTitle: When the savings are real, and when they aren't
slides.markdown:
Huffman's compression benefit is directly proportional to how skewed the input's symbol frequencies are. English text, where letter frequencies vary enormously (`e` and `t` vastly more common than `q` or `z`), sees real savings. A data source with near-uniform symbol frequencies gains almost nothing — Huffman's tree ends up close to balanced, meaning its code lengths converge toward what a fixed-length code would have given anyway.

This is worth knowing as a practical caveat, not just a theoretical one: proposing Huffman coding as a compression step is only a genuinely good idea when the actual data's frequency distribution is skewed enough to exploit — checking that assumption first is exactly the kind of judgment that separates "knows the algorithm" from "knows when the algorithm actually helps."
